The winter was brutal (I have the lingering eczema marks on my cheeks to prove it), which meant that I—and everyone else in the northern hemisphere—welcomed summer’s arrival with eager open arms, and plenty of open-toed footwear. Whether you land on the Birkenstock side of the sandal spectrum or wouldn’t be caught dead in less than a four-inch heel , the fact remains that the feet, and the toes, are out to play, and that means summer pedicures are an absolute must. Sure, the bare nails trend continues to reign supreme for your fingertips, but frankly, I feel a little exposed when my toenails are totally sans polish. Even if I’m feeling particularly minimalist, I’ll hit them with a quick swipe of clear or jelly polish before walking out the door. Since I also know that treating myself to a pedicure is one of those rare moments of total relaxation—for at least 30 minutes—I’ve been scouting for the shades the most stylish women in the city are wearing this season. Keep scrolling for the five hottest summer pedicure trends. Bright Whites, Big City It took me a while to embrace the white nail polish look, but now that milky polish is everywhere, I finally feel like I’m ready to join the (very chic) club. Manucurist Milky White $14 at Manucurist US My go-to brand for clean lacquer that actually nourishes my nails. I adore this slightly pearlescent white for an impossibly chic pedi. Essie Marshmallow $9.50 at Amazon US The GOAT of all milky white nail polishes, I’m never without this classic formula in my at-home nail kit . Flaunt It French Whoever said that French tips on the toes are passé hasn’t spent enough time strolling through Brooklyn. Every enviably dressed woman had the classic design peeking through her mesh flats. KISS Everlasting French Toenails Kit $32.66 at Amazon US Yes, press-ons for your toes exist, and they are the greatest hack for a flawless French pedicure in a flash. This kit has everything you need, with easy application tabs, to create the look without a salon appointment. Chanel 113 - FAUSSAIRE $34 at Chanel, Inc. A pinky rich nude that lasts and lasts, I always turn to this classic color for my French tip nails. Moody Mauve Mauve nails had a major moment this spring, and I’m happy to see that the cool-girl shade has stuck around for the summer. Zoya Nail Lacquer - Ryder $12 at Ulta Beauty A mauve-meets-brown shade that’s just begging to be worn with a pair of minimalist flip flops . essie Mismatch to Match $9.29 at Amazon US The perfect deep, dusty mauve—I can see myself wearing this all the way through summer and into fall—when, yes, I still make sure to keep my toes pedicured, even when they’re buried beneath cashmere socks. Pretty In Pink Think that pink isn’t for you? Try a chrome finish for an unexpected twist on the sweet shade. Nails, Inc. Mirror Chrome Nail Polish Feeling Chromatic $8.99 at Sally Beauty There’s no need to book a gel appointment for chrome nails when you have this gorgeous Barbie pink polish in your collection. ILNP Cosmetics, Inc. Yes Please $12.50 at Amazon US This pink holographic polish is practically its own accessory. I just need the perfect pair of black kitten heels to wear with it and I’m set for the summer. Dare to Bare Like I said, bare nails are everywhere right now, but I, and many of my beauty editor friends, have taken to swiping on a clear or barely-there polish to elevate the look. Manucurist Active Glow Raspberry $19 at Manucurist US Like a pH lip balm but for your nails, this nourishing formula provides that barely-there pink with one coat, and builds up to a jelly-like pink with a second and third layer. It’s sublime. OPI Start to Finish $14.99 at Amazon US A three-in-one polish that helps to strengthen your nails , prevent chipping, and deliver a deliciously glossy finish. Photograph: Reuters Iran Iran in talks with Oman over shipping but US negotiations on hold, says Tehran Iran discussing creation of temporary route through strait of Hormuz with its neighbour, says spokesperson Middle East crisis live – latest updates Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.52 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Iran has been in discussion with Oman about the creation of a new temporary route through the strait of Hormuz that would allow commercial shipping to resume, but is not yet reviving talks with the US, Tehran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said on Monday. Esmail Baghaei was responding to claims by Donald Trump that talks between the two sides covering all the major disputes between them could restart as early as Monday. Trump claimed he had held off from launching the biggest strike on any country “since world war two” over the weekend after Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, rang him to urge diplomacy. Trump said the cancellation was conditional on Iran reaching a deal quickly. Trump says Iran talks set for Monday as Tehran and Oman discuss strait of Hormuz deal Read more It is thought to be the 12th time in the war between the US and Iran that Trump has called off threatened strikes. Baghaei’s discussion of a new middle route through the strait of Homuz would represent progress. Iran is claiming full sovereignty over the strait and has been making demands over the routes and future management of the strait, including the possibility of charging fees in return for providing ships with maritime services. One proposal is to create an Omani-Iranian joint company that would provide all the services that insurance companies used to provide at high costs, but at lower prices, and with preferential tariffs for some countries. Unlocking a mutually acceptable route through the strait is the precondition to unlocking all the other agreements laid out in the memorandum of understanding, the ceasefire document both sides signed on 18 June. Disagreements about the memorandum’s obligations has led to a resumption of the war, which has spread to the Red Sea and to Iraq. Last week, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, said Iran was demanding that ships entering the strait take a route to the north close to Iran, but that some ships could take a southern route. Iran rejected the traffic being divided evenly between the two routes, and also that a third country could start de-mining the routes. Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran: “We are now talking about a corridor that will have a round trip route, not two or three separate routes. This intermediate route is to be used temporarily until a decision is made on a fixed route”. He framed the route as an alternative to the transport separation scheme, the previous longstanding prewar route overseen by the UN’s International Maritime Office. He said maps had been exchanged by the two sides. Baghaei stressed that the talks with Oman were bilateral and did not involve the US, adding that the negotiations with Oman had lasted seven to eight days. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, was not due to hold any talks with the US on Monday, he said. He said: “We are focused on reaching an understanding on a route that will ensure safe shipping traffic through the strait of Hormuz. Our effort is to determine a route at the earliest opportunity, with Oman’s consultation and cooperation; a route that will usually be temporary and based on which we can provide shipping in the strait of Hormuz.” He said an agreement on a route would not solve all the problems, pointing to the continuing US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, and that unless the US approach changed, there would be no significant improvement in the situation in the strait. Baghaei implied the talks with Oman would extend beyond a safe route to include future management of the strait. He said: “As a rule, in any understanding regarding shipping traffic between two coastal states, all issues related to the sovereignty and sovereign rights of the two countries, as well as issues of national security, national interests, and issues related to maritime services, are definitely considered and examined.” Recently there had been gloom in Omani circles about reaching an agreement with Iran on routes, leading to a revival of preparations for Oman’s European allies to start to clear the southern route of mines, a step that might have provoked direct conflict between Iran and European powers. Baghaei blamed the US for disregarding the memorandum of understanding by attempting to open up a southern route through Omani waters, arguing that article 5 of the memorandum specified that Iran alone within 30 days was required to return the level of shipping traffic to prewar conditions. He said ships that passed through this Oman route “were moving under pressure from Centcom [US Central Command], and due to intimidation from the American side. Some of these ships were even carrying military equipment, and in the shelter of these large ships sometimes frigates also travelled. “On 21 and 22 June, the US carried out widespread attacks against Iran and suddenly announced that everything was over under the pretext of the incident of seeing several ships in the strait of Hormuz,” he said. In a sign of the pressure Tehran diplomats face, a statement from the Assembly of Experts, the body of clerics that elects the supreme leader, warned against investing any trust in the US, saying: “Hope for understanding and agreement with this bullying regime will lead nowhere.” A section of the statement read: “It is incumbent upon all the free people in every corner of the world to keep aloft the banner of revenge and retribution for the martyred imam.” But the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he believed the “memorandum of understanding would prove to be the centre of gravity of our foreign relations in the future”. Saudi intervention came in a week in which Riyadh attacked Iranian-backed forces inside Iraq and raised the temperature in its dispute with the Iranian-backed Houthis in northern Yemen, underlining the extent to which Saudi Arabia fears the consequence of an all-out US war against Iran spiralling out of control across the Middle East. Romania has summoned Russia’s ambassador as it has reported that it shot down three drones in as many days. A Romanian plane shot down a drone after an incursion into the country’s airspace on Sunday morning, the Ministry of Defence reported. The incident followed similar interceptions on Friday and Saturday. list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Ukraine beheads its military as its performance begins to soar list 2 of 3 Romanian jet fighter shoots down suspected Russian drone list 3 of 3 At least 15 killed in Ukrainian and Russian strikes as holiday camp hit end of list Concern that Moscow’s war on Ukraine risks entangling neighbouring NATO states is on the rise. Romania is one of several alliance members to confront repeated stray drones recently, as Russia and Ukraine launch hundreds of the unmanned aircraft daily. Following Sunday’s incident, Bucharest summoned Russia’s ambassador to complain about the “repeated violations”, Foreign Minister Oana Toiu wrote on social media. Romania intercepted a Russian drone for the first time on Friday. That followed a similar incident on Saturday. An F-16 fighter jet then shot down an unmanned aircraft over the Black Sea on Sunday. President Nicusor Dan reported that an investigation had found that Friday’s drone was a “Shahed model, used by the Russian Federation in its war of aggression against Ukraine”. The persistent entry of Russian drones into the airspace of Eastern European countries is widely seen as a bid to test NATO and the European Union defences and reaction. “It is unacceptable and intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania’s airspace, which is also the airspace of NATO and the European Union,” US Army Colonel Martin O’Donnell, a senior NATO military spokesperson, wrote on social media following Sunday’s incident. Advertisement Romania, like other countries in the region, has seen frequent drone incursions since Russia launched its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. In late May, a drone struck an apartment building in the Romanian city of Galati, injuring two people. It was the first time such a strike hit a populated area in a NATO country. Last month , a maritime drone exploded in Romania’s Constanta port. The Baltic states have also reported repeated airspace violations in recent months, incursions that contributed to the collapse of Latvia’s government in May. NATO chief Mark Rutte has said Moscow’s “reckless behaviour is a danger to us all”. United States ambassador to NATO, Matthew Whitaker, has pledged the alliance will “defend every inch” of its territory. “NATO, Romania, and other nations [are actively acquiring] ground-based interceptors to enhance allied ⁠and national air defence capabilities,” O’Donnell noted. Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine continue to target one another with huge bombardments of drones and missiles. Ballistic missiles hit Kyiv and other cities overnight on Sunday morning, killing two people and wounding at least three. Russia’s Defence Ministry, which persistently insists that it does not target civilians, said the attack on Kyiv struck sites linked to drone production. In Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine, authorities said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed four civilians in the city of Horlivka. According to Ivan Prikhodko, the city’s Russian-appointed mayor, the city had come under fire in the early hours of Sunday. Russia’s Defence Ministry has said that overnight, it struck down 133 Ukrainian drones over Russia, the Black Sea and Crimea. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9w.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Yabloko chairmain Nikolai Rybakov was at the hearing in Moscow By Laura Gozzi Â and Â Sergey Goryashko Published 32 minutes ago Russia's only liberal, anti-war party will not be able to take part in next month's parliamentary elections, a Moscow court has ruled. Yabloko was the only registered party to oppose Russia's war on Ukraine. The case against it was brought forward by Rodina, a pro-Kremlin nationalist party. Hundreds of people - mostly very young - on Monday had stood outside the Moscow courthouse where the hearing was taking place in support of Yabloko, singing songs and waving flags. Videos posted on social media showed that when news of the verdict spread among the crowd, many started chanting: "Shame! Shame!" The lawsuit by the Rodina party accused Yabloko of publicly supporting an extremist organisation by publishing material on its website in support of the "international LGBT movement", which Russia's Supreme Court designated as extremist in 2023. Rodina also said Yabloko was guilty of copyright infringement after a senior party member had quoted the lyrics of a Soviet-era song - "Let there always be sunshine" - in an interview. At the hearing, Russia's financial monitoring service also claimed that Yabloko received money through third parties from foreign countries, including Germany and the US. The Kremlin-controlled Central Electoral Commission had approved Yabloko's candidate list in late July. But by then several party members had already been barred from running, including two deputy chairmen and deputy leader Maxim Kruglov, who was sentenced in June to seven years' imprisonment for social media posts about civilian casualties in Bucha, Mariupol and other Ukrainian cities. And last week, Yabloko had suffered a cyberattack soon after launching a donations appeal for its election campaign fund. It campaigned under the slogan "For peace and freedom! For a life without fear!" and advocated for a "ceasefire, diplomacy, and peace" and "for a Russia free from fear and political repression". Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Hundreds of young Russians gathered on Monday in support of Yabloko Hundreds gathered outside the Moscow courthouse, chanting "Russia" and "Yabloko" - the Russian word for "apple" - as the eight-hour hearing dragged on. Many carried apples as a sign of support. Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, any remaining opposition to the Kremlin has been crushed. Public shows of dissent have been suppressed by wartime censorship laws and can trigger hefty fines or long prison sentences. Because protests are no longer permitted, the Yabloko hearing offered a rare chance for likeminded Russians opposing the war to gather publicly. "For Yabloko. For freedom" was scribbled in chalk on the pavement outside the courthouse. Yabloko has not won Duma seats since 2003 but has contested every election since. Once led by presidential contender Grigory Yavlinsky, it later fractured with allies - expelling the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny in 2007 and criticising him even after he was eventually imprisoned ahead of his death in 2024. Still, Yabloko remained Russia's most consistent anti-war voice, opposing Russia's war on Chechnya, the 2014 annexation of Crimea, and the invasion of Ukraine. With ruling party United Russia's ratings down to 33% amid inflation, internet blackouts and drone strikes, Yabloko's support had been surging. The Kremlin could have allowed Yabloko to contest the election and initially appeared to be leaning in that direction, potentially to use the party's marginal result in 2021 - when it won just 1.34% of the vote - to demonstrate how unpopular an anti-war stance is in Russia. But the Kremlin appears to have changed its calculations as signs of growing dissent over the war in Ukraine emerge. Without a political force that clearly represents the opposition on the ballot, fewer people may be motivated to go to the polls. A low-turnout election, particularly among those who oppose the ruling party, is exactly what the Kremlin wants. All 10 other parties taking part in the election either support the war in Ukraine or do not openly criticise it. And although United Russia's ratings appear to be in a deep dive, the Kremlin still has the resources to deliver the outcome it wants at the election. Independent election watchdogs have been deprived of much of their ability to monitor and challenge the process. https://jowhar.com/slovakia-sets-new-42-.text: Home NEWS WORLD NEWS ARTICLE POLITICS SPORT Somali TV Quran karim NEWS ARTICLE WORLD NEWS POLITICS Sport QURAN Video Somali TV privacy-policy terms and conditions Home NEWS WORLD NEWS ARTICLE POLITICS SPORT Somali TV Quran karim WORLD NEWS Facebook X Telegram WhatsApp ReddIt Pinterest Digg The records come during an exceptional spell of hot weather and low rainfall across central Europe Central Europe’s heatwave tightened its grip on Friday as Slovakia shattered its all-time temperature record for a second consecutive day, with thermometers hitting 42.2C in a southern village, the national weather agency reported. The new peak was measured in Dolne Plachtince, surpassing the previous record of 41.4C set a day earlier in southwestern Slovakia, according to a statement from the Slovak Hydrometeorological Institute (SHMU) sent to journalists. The back-to-back records underscore an exceptional stretch of searing temperatures paired with scarce rainfall across central Europe. In Slovakia alone, the country’s longstanding temperature mark has now been broken twice in June, highlighting how rapidly conditions have escalated during the current spell. Austria, Slovakia’s neighbour to the west, has also registered record-breaking heat twice this week. Experts say climate change has amplified drought across Europe this summer, with prolonged extreme heat fueling unusually dry ground and worsening water stress. The same mix of high temperatures and drought has continued to drive wildfires across the region, including in Serbia, where a man died in a village about 80km east of Belgrade after losing control of a fire he lit near his home. In central Serbia’s Ibar valley, a major forest fire remained out of control, with firefighters supported by water-bombing aircraft battling difficult terrain as they tried to shield nearby villages. Local media footage showed thick smoke rising from pine forests as flames tore across hillsides close to homes. Smoke from another wildfire, burning in a nature reserve northeast of the capital, was visible from the city. Farther south, Albanian authorities said they had brought dozens of blazes under control after fires in the south of the country prompted a small number of evacuations. Across most of the region, authorities have issued warnings of extreme fire danger. Serbian police said the death of the man who was overwhelmed by the blaze he started underscored the need to respect fire bans. “This is the most serious consequence of irresponsible behaviour, and I therefore once again call on all citizens to exercise the utmost caution,” police officer Luka Causic said. Meanwhile, days of relentless heat have further deepened drought conditions affecting large swathes of Europe. Sections of the Danube have fallen to record-low levels, constraining hydropower generation and complicating oil imports transported by river in Serbia. At the Bezdan monitoring station, where the Danube enters from Croatia and Hungary, measurements showed the river continuing to recede after reaching record lows last week. An investment agreement for this major project was signed on Friday by the Lithuanian Ministry of the Economy and Innovation and DEMZ, a Ukrainian defense sector company. "By actively supporting Ukraine, Lithuania is strengthening Ukraine's defense-and, in turn, the defense of our own country and the entire eastern flank. Today, we see that our support for Ukraine is also generating tangible economic dividends," said the President. The Lithuanian leader emphasized that the agreements signed today at the Office of the Government of the Republic of Lithuania will contribute to long-term economic and competence development in Alytus and Prienai District and create new jobs. In 2024, the Presidents of Lithuania and Ukraine signed a comprehensive ten-year agreement on security cooperation. In early 2026, they signed an agreement on the development of joint defense projects in Lithuania. Under the newly signed agreements, a regional production and innovation center of DEMZ, a Ukrainian defense sector company, will be established in Lithuania. The center will develop and test new products that meet NATO standards. The President's Communication Group
